Test whether prevalence is above or below a decision threshold

Source: R/test_threshold.R
test_threshold.Rd

Analysis function: given the number of positives and the number tested at one or more sites, tests whether the true prevalence is above (or below) a decision threshold, with an exact binomial test (default) or a Wald z-test. Returns the p-value, whether the result is significant, and the confidence interval for the true prevalence that matches the test: Clopper-Pearson for the exact test, Wald for the Wald test. It is the analysis twin of design_threshold().

With a perfect diagnostic test, the share of people who test positive is the prevalence, and it is compared with the threshold directly. With an imperfect test it is not: some people with the condition test negative, and some without it test positive. So the threshold is converted to the share who would test positive if the true prevalence were exactly at the threshold, \(\theta \cdot Se + (1 - \theta)(1 - Sp)\), where \(\theta\) is the threshold, \(Se\) the sensitivity and \(Sp\) the specificity. For example, with a threshold of 5 percent, sensitivity 0.9 and specificity 0.95: of the 5 percent who have the condition, 0.9 test positive (0.045), and of the 95 percent who do not, 0.05 wrongly test positive (0.0475), so 9.25 percent would test positive. The test then asks whether the share testing positive is far enough above 9.25 percent that chance alone is unlikely to explain it: with 100 people tested, 12 positives (12 percent) is not enough (p = 0.21), but 15 (15 percent) is (p = 0.04). This works because, when \(Se + Sp\) is above 1, a higher true prevalence always gives a higher share testing positive. The prevalence and its interval are then converted back to the true scale (Rogan-Gladen correction). Clustering is allowed for with a design effect, as in estimate_prevalence().

Hypotheses (\(p\) is the true prevalence, \(\theta\) the threshold):

"greater" (default)

H0: \(p \le \theta\) against H1: \(p > \theta\): is prevalence above the threshold?

"less"

H0: \(p \ge \theta\) against H1: \(p < \theta\): is prevalence below the threshold?

"two.sided"

H0: \(p = \theta\) against H1: \(p \ne \theta\). A threshold question is usually one-way (above or below), so "greater" or "less" is usually the right choice.

Usage

test_threshold(
  x,
  n,
  threshold,
  alternative = c("greater", "less", "two.sided"),
  sensitivity = 1,
  specificity = 1,
  conf_level = 0.95,
  icc = NULL,
  method = c("exact", "wald")
)

Arguments

x

Vector of whole-number counts of people who tested positive, one per site (a single number for one site).

n

Vector of whole-number totals tested, one per site (same length as x).

threshold

Decision threshold for the true prevalence, strictly between 0 and 1 (for example 0.05 for the WHO pfhrp2/3 deletion threshold).

alternative

Direction of the test: "greater" (default, prevalence above the threshold), "less" (below it) or "two.sided" (different from it).

sensitivity

Diagnostic sensitivity in (0, 1]; default 1 (the test never misses a case).

specificity

Diagnostic specificity in (0, 1]; default 1 (the test never gives a false positive). sensitivity + specificity must exceed 1.

conf_level

Confidence level for the interval, in (0, 1); default 0.95. The significance level of the test is 1 - conf_level.

icc

Optional. Intra-cluster correlation (ICC), in [0, 1]. If NULL (default), it is estimated from the sites. Set to 0 for no clustering. A supplied value is also used with only one site (see Details).

method

"exact" (default): exact binomial test with the Clopper-Pearson interval. "wald": Wald z-test with the Wald interval. Each interval is its own test turned around, so reject is TRUE exactly when threshold is outside the interval, whichever method is used.

Value

A list with:

p_value

p-value for the chosen alternative.

reject

TRUE if p_value is below 1 - conf_level.

prevalence

Estimated true prevalence (Rogan-Gladen corrected, between 0 and 1).

ci_lower, ci_upper

Confidence interval for the true prevalence; ci_upper is 1 for "greater" and ci_lower is 0 for "less".

n_eff

Effective sample size, sum(n) / deff.

icc

ICC used: as supplied, or estimated from the data.

deff

Design effect used (1 with no clustering).

Details

Design effect (returned as deff). It is \(1 + (n_w - 1) ICC\), where \(n_w = \sum n^2 / \sum n\) is the mean number of people per site, weighted by site size. With icc supplied (for example from earlier surveys), that value is used. Supply icc with one site only when the site stands for a wider population, such as a district; if the site itself is the population of interest, leave icc = NULL. With icc = NULL, the ICC is estimated from the data as in estimate_prevalence(); this needs at least two sites, and with one site the design effect is 1.

Effective sample size. \(m\) (returned as n_eff) is the number tested divided by the design effect. The number of positives is scaled the same way, to \(\hat{p} m\), where \(\hat{p} = \sum x / \sum n\) is the measured prevalence. Neither need be a whole number: the binomial tail probabilities are worked out through the beta distribution, which equals pbinom() for whole numbers.

Exact test (method = "exact"). Suppose the true prevalence is exactly at the threshold. For "greater", the p-value is the chance of at least as many positives as observed; for "less", the chance of at most as many. The threshold is first converted to the measured scale, \(\theta_{app} = \theta \cdot Se + (1 - \theta)(1 - Sp)\). With one site and a design effect of 1, the one-sided p-values are exactly those of R's binom.test().

Wald test (method = "wald"). The normal approximation,

$$z = \frac{\hat{p} - \theta_{app}}{\sqrt{\hat{p}(1 - \hat{p}) / m}}$$

with the standard error worked out at the measured prevalence \(\hat{p}\). The one-sided p-values are the normal tail areas above and below \(z\). It can be too optimistic for small samples or a prevalence near 0; with no positives (or all positive) the standard error is 0, and any threshold on the other side counts as rejected.

Two-sided p-value. For both methods, twice the smaller of the two one-sided p-values, at most 1. For the exact test this is the "central" two-sided exact test (Fay 2010), the one that matches the two-sided Clopper-Pearson interval. It is cautious: the false alarm rate is at most 1 - conf_level, and often well below it. It can differ from binom.test(), which adds up all counts that are less likely than the one observed.

Interval. The interval is the test turned around: it holds the thresholds the test would not reject, so reject is TRUE exactly when threshold is outside it. It is matched to alternative: \([L, 1]\) for "greater", \([0, U]\) for "less", and the two-sided interval (\(\alpha/2\) in each tail) for "two.sided". For the exact test it is the Clopper-Pearson interval,

$$L = B^{-1}(\alpha;\; x_{eff},\; m - x_{eff} + 1), \qquad U = B^{-1}(1 - \alpha;\; x_{eff} + 1,\; m - x_{eff})$$

with \(x_{eff} = \hat{p} m\) and \(B^{-1}\) the beta quantile function; for the Wald test it is \(\hat{p} \pm z_{1-\alpha} \sqrt{\hat{p}(1 - \hat{p}) / m}\) (\(\alpha/2\) in place of \(\alpha\) for two-sided). It is built on the measured scale and then corrected for an imperfect test, with ends kept within [0, 1]; if the whole corrected interval lies outside [0, 1], the function warns that the data do not fit the assumed sensitivity and specificity.

When to use DRpower instead. With the ICC supplied, this function keeps the chance of a false alarm at or below the significance level. With icc = NULL and few sites of very different sizes, the ICC is poorly estimated and the false alarm rate can be well above it (13 to 28 percent at a 5 percent level in simulation); with an ICC estimated from few sites it also has low power. For pfhrp2/3 deletion surveys with several sites and an unknown ICC, where the question is whether prevalence is above the threshold, consider DRpower (https://mrc-ide.github.io/DRpower/). It estimates prevalence and ICC together and has more power, especially with few sites, but more false alarms when prevalence is close to the threshold.

References

MMS-SD Study Design Workshop. https://mrc-ide.github.io/MMS-SD_workshop/

Clopper, C. J. & Pearson, E. S. (1934) The use of confidence or fiducial limits illustrated in the case of the binomial. Biometrika 26(4), 404-413. doi:10.1093/biomet/26.4.404

Fay, M. P. (2010) Two-sided exact tests and matching confidence intervals for discrete data. The R Journal 2(1), 53-58. doi:10.32614/RJ-2010-008

Kish, L. (1965) Survey Sampling. Wiley. (Design effect.)

Rogan, W. J. & Gladen, B. (1978) Estimating prevalence from the results of a screening test. American Journal of Epidemiology 107(1), 71-76. doi:10.1093/oxfordjournals.aje.a112510

See also

design_threshold

Examples

# One site: is prevalence above 5 percent?
test_threshold(x = 8, n = 100, threshold = 0.05)
#> $p_value
#> [1] 0.1279605
#> 
#> $reject
#> [1] FALSE
#> 
#> $prevalence
#> [1] 0.08
#> 
#> $ci_lower
#> [1] 0.04042887
#> 
#> $ci_upper
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> $n_eff
#> [1] 100
#> 
#> $icc
#> [1] 0
#> 
#> $deff
#> [1] 1
#> 

# Five sites, ICC estimated from the data
test_threshold(
  x = c(0, 6, 1, 11, 4),
  n = c(50, 60, 40, 80, 70),
  threshold = 0.05
)
#> $p_value
#> [1] 0.174857
#> 
#> $reject
#> [1] FALSE
#> 
#> $prevalence
#> [1] 0.07333333
#> 
#> $ci_lower
#> [1] 0.03752174
#> 
#> $ci_upper
#> [1] 1
#> 
#> $n_eff
#> [1] 112.8
#> 
#> $icc
#> [1] 0.02662419
#> 
#> $deff
#> [1] 2.659574
#> 

# Two-sided, imperfect diagnostic test
test_threshold(x = 12, n = 100, threshold = 0.10,
               alternative = "two.sided",
               sensitivity = 0.9, specificity = 0.95)
#> $p_value
#> [1] 0.795509
#>

#>

#> [1] 100
#> 
#> $icc
#> [1] 0
#> 
#> $deff
#> [1] 1
#> 

# One site, a clear result: the interval lies above the threshold
test_threshold(x = 15, n = 100, threshold = 0.05)
#> $p_value
#> [1] 0.0001358542

#> [1] 1
#> 

# Wald test and interval instead of the exact test
test_threshold(x = 15, n = 100, threshold = 0.05, method = "wald")
